Abstract Understanding how AI is reshaping work requires an accurate account of the tasks workers perform. Workers are often the first to see how their jobs are changing, as new responsibilities and tools often appear in everyday work before these changes reach formal descriptions. Interviews with workers can help capture these emerging changes in job tasks. Yet existing methods support standardized ratings across workers, while open-ended conversations with workers remain costly to collect and synthesize at scale. We introduce the Stanford Task Network (TaskNet), an occupational taxonomy grounded directly in workers’ accounts of their everyday work. To construct TaskNet, we develop a mixed-initiative system that induces task inventories directly from workers. The system conducts interviews, standardizes reports into individual task lists, and aggregates these lists into occupational task inventories. Applied to six occupations spanning a range of education requirements and AI exposure, our system interviews 132 workers and produces 202 task statements from 2726 reports, all of which were accepted by O * NET Center analysts, compared to roughly 65% of workers’ write-in task suggestions collected through the current O * NET data collection process, a major alternative source for emerging tasks. Every statement is validated by 318 incumbents in 7923 ratings of relevance and importance. Relative to the task data from the O * NET 31.0 database for the sampled occupations, TaskNet covers 75% of the 118 published O * NET tasks and adds 79 tasks with no O * NET counterpart and 58 that refine existing statements. It covers 89% of tasks reported by held-out workers, compared with 79% for O * NET, and a larger share of the activities described in employer job postings (72.5% vs. 70.2%). Downstream, TaskNet changes AI exposure estimates in both directions, raising them for Software Developers and Lawyers, two occupations where AI’s effects are widely debated. Because such estimates guide workforce policy and training, more complete and up-to-date task lists can help direct these efforts toward the workers most likely to be affected. TaskNet provides a foundation for keeping occupational information current and grounded in workers’ experiences as AI reshapes work.
1 Introduction Thirty years ago, the Occupational Information Network (O * NET) was created with an ambitious goal: to prepare workers and the institutions that train and employ them for a rapidly changing economy. Workers needed to understand how their skills translated to new opportunities, educators needed to know what capabilities to develop, and employers needed a common language for 1
describing the work they needed done. O * NET became the main source of occupational information in the U.S., providing systematic descriptions of more than 900 occupations, including the tasks workers perform and the knowledge and skills those tasks require (Peterson et al., 1999). Today, O * NET’s mission has taken on new importance. As AI systems expand their capabilities on economically relevant tasks, researchers and policymakers need occupational information that is both current and granular (Autor et al., 2024, Denain et al., 2026). Task inventories have long been used to study how technology changes work activities and, through them, labor demand (Acemoglu and Restrepo, 2019, Autor and Handel, 2013, Autor et al., 2003). Researchers now rely extensively on O * NET task statements to estimate AI exposure (Brynjolfsson et al., 2018, Eloundou et al., 2024, Felten et al., 2021, Putka et al., 2026, Webb, 2020), characterize AI use (Chatterji et al., 2025, Handa et al., 2025, Tomlinson et al., 2025), and study AI’s effects on employment (Brynjolfsson et al., 2025a). The quality of these analyses depends on how occupational tasks are collected. O * NET primarily gathers task information through structured surveys of workers and occupational experts. Incum- bents receive a list of task statements, rate each for relevance, frequency, and importance, and may write in tasks the list omits (Dierdorff and Norton, 2011). Surveys provide standardized measurements of known tasks but are less suited to discovering work not already represented in the inventory. Interviews offer a complementary approach. Rather than asking workers to react to pre-written statements, interviews allow them to describe their work in their own words. Workers can explain how they perform their responsibilities in practice, identify activities that are new or changing, and elaborate on them through follow-up questions. This makes interviews especially valuable for surfacing work that existing task lists or employee-facing records may not capture. Until recently, conducting and synthesizing interviews at scale was prohibitively costly. Language models now make both more feasible. AI interviewers can elicit detailed worker accounts through open-ended conversations and follow-ups. AI can also support concept discovery and aggregation to organize those accounts into a task taxonomy (Section 2). We bring these capabilities together in the Stanford Task Network (TaskNet) Interviewer, an adaptive interview system that induces occupational task inventories from workers’ accounts of their everyday work. Turning these accounts into comprehensive, comparable task inventories raises two challenges. First, workers tend to describe their work through episodes and anecdotes rather than discrete tasks, so the interviewer must elicit task-level detail and cover the full range of responsibilities without leading the worker. The TaskNet Interviewer tracks coverage of a topic guide and infers a likely task inventory from the worker’s role to probe tasks not yet mentioned. Second, interviews do not deliver the comparability that surveys get by design. Tasks reported by different workers must be combined into a single inventory, which means merging paraphrases, reconciling differences in granularity, and preserving infrequent but genuine tasks. Standard embedding-based clustering is poorly suited to this, because textual similarity does not track whether two reports describe the same work, nor at what level of detail they should count as one task. The TaskNet Interviewer aggregates tasks through an iterative procedure that adapts hierarchical task analysis and functional job analysis to language-model clustering. Each task statement remains traceable to the interview excerpts that support it. We apply the TaskNet Interviewer to six occupations—Personal Care Aides, Software Developers, El- ementary School Teachers, Except Special Education, Emergency Medicine Physicians, Dishwashers, and Lawyers—selected to span education and training requirements and AI exposure, with recently updated O * NET task data and clear occupational boundaries. From interviews with 132 workers (20– 25 per occupation), we construct TaskNet, a taxonomy of 202 task statements synthesized from 2726 task reports. Trained O * NET Center analysts judge all 202 TaskNet statements valid under O * NET ’s standards, making them eligible for review as Emerging Tasks. Another 318 incumbents (31–69 2
per occupation) provide 7923 ratings of task importance, time spent, verifiability, and variation in performance, enriching the inventory for analyses of task differences and AI exposure. Compared with O * NET, TaskNet identifies 79 new and 58 refined tasks while covering 75% of existing task statements (Section 4.3). It also covers more tasks reported by held-out workers (89.3% vs. 78.6%; higher in five of six occupations) and more activities in employer job postings (72.5% vs. 70.2%; higher in four of six; Section 5.2). These differences affect downstream AI exposure estimates (Putka et al., 2026). Under both the measures of Eloundou et al. (2024) and Tomei and Teeselink (2026), TaskNet raises exposure scores relative to O * NET for Lawyers, Software Developers, and Elementary School Teachers, but lowers them for Personal Care Aides. Much of this difference comes from newly identified coordination and oversight tasks. Although these tasks are highly exposed to AI, their reliance on human accountability and tacit knowledge suggests that such exposure may reflect complementarity as much as substitution. Finer-grained task descriptions also distinguish exposed from unexposed activities that O * NET combines into broader tasks. Thus, task inventories shape both the overall level of estimated AI exposure and its distribution within occupations. Beyond these six occupations, TaskNet offers a repeatable approach to updating occupational task data from workers’ accounts. Extending the method across occupations and repeating it over time could reveal emerging responsibilities and changes in established tasks, providing a worker-centered complement to existing occupational data. Our contributions are as follows:
1. We introduce the TaskNet Interviewer (Section 3.1), a mixed-initiative system that elicits tasks through semi-structured interviews with adaptive task probing, and verifies them through worker review. To our knowledge, we are the first to build occupational task inventories directly from workers’ own accounts in AI-conducted interviews.
2. We present a task aggregation framework that derives an occupational task inventory from individual task lists (Section 3.2). The framework separates the definition of a task from the aggregation procedure, allowing task definitions to be revised while maintaining coverage and keeping tasks distinct.
3. We propose a framework for evaluating task inventories as representations of occupational work. Because there is no ground truth for task lists, we triangulate across stakeholders and independent sources to test whether the inventory captures the work workers do.
4. We release TaskNet, a worker-grounded taxonomy of 202 validated tasks across six occupations. Relative to O * NET 31.0, it adds 79 newly identified tasks and 58 refinements, achieving higher coverage and finer granularity.
5. We find that TaskNet produces different AI exposure estimates than O * NET, with the largest increases for Lawyers and Software Developers and a decrease for Personal Care Aides. These differences highlight how more comprehensive and detailed task inventories can sharpen our understanding of where and how AI may affect work.
2 Related Work Task inventories Task lists have traditionally been built by job analysts through labor-intensive observation and analysis. Examples include the four editions of the Dictionary of Occupational Titles from 1939-1991 (Miller et al., 1980, Peterson et al., 1999, U.S. Department of Labor, Employment and Training Administration, 1991) and the U.S. Air Force task inventories (Christal, 1974, Christal and Weissmuller, 1988, Ramsey-Klee, 1984). These efforts grounded task lists in direct study of workers but were costly to sustain across many occupations. O * NET broadens the sources of task information, 3
drawing on surveys, write-in task statements, AI-assisted subject matter expert input, and other data sources (Advisory Panel for the Dictionary of Occupational Titles, 1993, Dierdorff and Norton, 2011, Klein et al., 2025, Lewis et al., 2025). Candidate tasks undergo review by occupational analysts before entering the inventory in a later survey cycle. TaskNet introduces AI-conducted interviews as a complementary source of task statements, producing statements that meet O
*
NET’s standards
and can enter its existing review process. More recently, researchers have used language models to augment occupational data. Putka et al. (2023) predict the knowledge, skills, abilities, and other characteristics (KSAOs) associated with occupations, Lewis and Morris (2024) predict additional task information, and Lewis et al. (2025) generate candidate tasks for drone manufacturing. Klein et al. (2025) describe the use of language models to assist O * NET analysts in reviewing write-in task statements. In these applications, language models either generate occupational information from their own knowledge or help process statements that workers have already submitted. In TaskNet, workers provide the content of each task, while the model guides the conversation and structures what workers report. Separately, researchers have applied natural language processing methods to extract occupational information from job postings (Howison et al., 2025), including skills (Atalay et al., 2020, Deming and Kahn, 2018). These approaches speed up the production of occupational data, but rely on model knowledge or employer-provided text rather than the workers who perform the tasks. TaskNet brings these strands together. Like the computational approaches, it uses language models to make the production of occupational data faster and cheaper. Like O * NET, it takes a human- centered approach, grounding task lists in incumbents’ own accounts. LLM-Based Interviewing Recent advances in language models have enabled flexible systems for conducting semi-structured or adaptive interviews, ranging from single-LLM approaches guided by prompting (Geiecke and Jaravel, 2024, Park et al., 2026, Wuttke et al., 2025) to multi-agent systems (Anugraha et al., 2026, Liu and Yu, 2025, Talaei et al., 2025). Many applications of LLM-based interviews focus on qualitative accounts of respondents’ attitudes, experiences, and perspectives (Cuevas et al., 2024, Wong et al., 2025, Wuttke et al., 2025), with more recent work extending to professionals’ descriptions of their work (Anthropic, 2025). We build on this literature to elicit occupational tasks, drawing on mixed-initiative interaction (Horvitz, 1999, Ziems et al., 2025) and conversational interviewing (Schober and Conrad, 1997). AI-Assisted Qualitative Analysis Prior work uses language models to organize and synthesize open-ended text, including developing qualitative codebooks (Dai et al., 2023), inducing inter- pretable concepts (Lam et al., 2024), and identifying latent topics (Pham et al., 2024). Related methods extract recurring patterns from large conversational datasets (Tamkin et al., 2024) and cluster semantically related observations (Viswanathan et al., 2024, Zhang et al., 2023).
3 System Design The TaskNet Interviewer builds an occupational task inventory in three stages. Discovery interviews individual workers and produces and verifies a task list for each worker (Section 3.1). Aggregation consolidates these lists into a single candidate inventory for the occupation (Section 3.2). Validation brings in job analysts to review the inventory and workers to rate its tasks (Section 3.3).
4
We designed this system around three guiding principles. First, workers are the authority on their own work. Every task in the inventory originates in an activity reported by workers during discovery. Second, task statements meet the standard that the O * NET Center applies in its own emerging tasks process. This allows newly discovered tasks to enter the same adoption process as existing O * NET tasks and preserves compatibility with the broader Occupational Information Network. Third, the inventory must support analyses that aggregate over tasks. Such analyses require task statements to be consistent in granularity, collectively exhaustive of the work workers reported, and sufficiently distinct to prevent the same work from being counted twice.
3.1 Task Discovery Task discovery aims to create a comprehensive task list for each worker. The challenge with creating exhaustive task lists is that a worker’s first account of a job is rarely exhaustive (Morgeson and Campion, 1997). Workers are more likely to report recent or salient tasks while overlooking activities that are routine, infrequent, or taken for granted. Discovery therefore cannot simply record what workers volunteer. We therefore treat task discovery as an active elicitation problem. To maximize coverage of the worker’s task set, we apply a mixed-initiative design in which the interviewer helps the worker recall and elaborate on their responsibilities, a model constructs a candidate task list from the conversation and proposes likely missing tasks, and the worker confirms or revises the result (see Figure 1). Building on SparkMe (Anugraha et al., 2026), our task induction system introduces three design innovations to a multi-agent framework for adaptive semi-structured interviews that tracks topic-guide coverage, incorporates emerging themes, and manages interview length. First, we define topic coverage by tasks. Typically, in semi-structured interviews, a topic may be considered complete once the participant has addressed it. For task induction, this standard is insufficient: a participant can respond to every topic in broad terms (e.g., “I see patients”) while yielding few concrete tasks. We therefore define coverage at the level of the task. A topic is complete only once the participant’s response targets the granularity of an O * NET task statement. Each coverage criterion evaluates the response in terms of the tasks it specifies. When a participant names 5
a responsibility, tool, or stakeholder without describing the tasks it entails, the interviewer follows up to develop that description into concrete tasks. Second, we search for uncovered tasks through adaptive task probing. An interviewer can adapt to themes that emerge in conversation, but it cannot pursue tasks that never surface in the first place. Adaptive task probing addresses this gap by using knowledge of the worker’s role to identify plausible omissions. Throughout the interview, the system maintains a running list of reported tasks. Separately, it infers a candidate task set for the worker’s described role. This inventory draws on the model’s prior knowledge of the role, conditioned on the conversation. The interviewer then compares these two lists and turns the most relevant gaps into open-ended follow-up questions. Finally, we present the induced task list for worker verification. Because recognizing a task is generally easier than recalling it (Mandler, 1980), job analysis has long relied on inventories that incumbents review rather than requiring them to generate complete lists from scratch (Christal, 1974). Our approach preserves that advantage while personalizing the inventory to each worker. The system consolidates the reported tasks at O * NET granularity and proposes additional tasks implied by the interview. Across the 132 interviews that contribute to our six task inventories, workers reviewed 2798 proposed tasks, of which they confirmed 94.2% unchanged, revised 5.3% , deleted 0.5%, and added 163 of their own.
3.2 Task Aggregation Interviews provide rich accounts of work, but workers use different vocabulary and levels of detail, making their reports difficult to compare. Similar wording can describe distinct tasks, such as preparing meals and feeding clients, while different wording can describe the same task, such as recording vitals in an EHR and writing blood pressure in a care log. Aggregation must therefore resolve both task identity—whether reports describe the same work—and task granularity—the level of detail at which that work should be represented. We introduce a framework that makes these boundary decisions explicit and produces standardized task inventories. O * NET’s guidelines specify how to formulate task statements but leave task boundaries largely to analyst judgment. Our framework separates the definition of a task from the aggregation procedure, allowing researchers
to inspect boundary decisions and adapt the definition to different measurement needs. Our definition combines hierarchical task analysis (HTA) and functional job analysis (FJA). HTA organizes work into goals and the actions used to achieve them, providing a basis for identifying reports of the same task (Annett and Duncan, 1967, Stanton, 2006). Because goals nest, however, HTA alone does not establish a consistent level of granularity (Stanton, 2006). FJA helps establish that level by distinguishing workers’ actions from their tools, materials, and settings (Fine and Cronshaw, 1999, Fine and Wiley, 1971). Together, these principles define a task as the highest node in a goal hierarchy whose subtasks differ only in context. Thus, recording vitals in different systems constitutes one task, while preparing meals and feeding clients remain distinct. Unlike similarity-based clustering, this criterion explicitly distinguishes differences in action from differences in context (Steck et al., 2024, Zhou et al., 2022). We apply this definition through four iterative steps: clustering, synthesis, overlap resolution, and coverage checking. First, we cluster worker reports by task identity and granularity, retaining only clusters reported by at least two workers, following O * NET’s emerging-tasks rule (Klein et al., 2025). Second, a language model synthesizes each cluster into a task statement using O
*
NET’s guidelines (National Center for O*NET Development, 2009) and writing principles developed with feedback from O * NET Center staff. Each statement generalizes only as far as its source reports support and 6
is split if it combines distinct tasks. Third, an LLM judge checks pairs of statements for overlap: duplicate or nested statements are merged, and partially overlapping statements are reworded to separate their scopes. Finally, an LLM judge checks whether the revised statements still cover their source reports. Uncovered and unclustered reports are reassigned where possible; the remainder enter another round, continuing while new shared tasks emerge. We then manually compare each statement with its source reports and correct omissions or distortions. These steps preserve distinct, measurable tasks while recovering coverage that may be lost during synthesis and revision.
3.3 Task Validation We use a multi-stakeholder validation procedure that pairs O * NET analyst reviews with worker ratings. Job analysts assess task-writing quality and occupational fit, while workers assess whether the tasks reflect their jobs. These two assessments evaluate adherence to O * NET’s standards and fidelity to workers’ accounts in line with our guiding principles. Two trained job analysts at the O * NET Center jointly reviewed every statement using O * NET’s task-review procedure (Lewis et al., 2025). They reached consensus on three questions: does the statement describe a task, does it meet O * NET’s writing guidelines (National Center for O*NET Development, 2009), and is the work primarily performed by the target occupation? Their judgments distinguish valid occupational tasks from adjacent tasks—valid work that would not belong in the target occupation’s task list. We revised flagged statements in consultation with the analysts. Workers assessed each statement on O * NET’s dimensions of relevance, importance, and frequency (National Center for O*NET Development, 2026b). We retain tasks rated relevant by at least a quarter of incumbents. Among retained tasks, those with relevance of at least 67% and mean importance of at least 3 are classified as core, and the remainder are supplemental. Workers also rated five additional, established properties relevant to AI capabilities, including duration (Kwa and Cheng, 2025, Mertens et al., 2026), expertise requirements (Autor and Thompson, 2025), and verifiability (Polanyi, 1966) (Section E.1; Section K). Each worker rated a subset of statements to limit survey fatigue, with adaptive assignment balancing the number of ratings across tasks (Jeong et al., 2023).
4 Task Inventories for Six Occupations To test the TaskNet Interviewer, we recruited workers from six occupations in the O * NET-SOC Taxonomy: Personal Care Aides (31-1122.00), Software Developers (15-1252.00), Elementary School Teachers, Except Special Education (25-2021.00), Emergency Medicine Physicians (29-1214.00), Dishwashers (35-9021.00), and Lawyers (23-1011.00) 1 . We selected these occupations based on three criteria: the recency of their O * NET task information (maximum of three years old with majority updated in 2025), their diversity in job zone 2 and AI exposure (see Section 7), and low ambiguity of their occupational titles. The last criterion avoids, for example, titles such as Accountants and Auditors (13-2011.00), for which respondents may conflate distinct specializations.

4.1 Respondent Sample We recruited workers through Mercor Inc., an AI human data company. Workers reside and work in the 50 U.S. states and the District of Columbia, excluding California. Individuals living and working in Puerto Rico and other U.S. territories are not included. Most participants came from Mercor’s existing platform population, while Dishwashers were also recruited externally through job-posting sites. A language model first identified likely occupational matches from candidates’ work histories and O * NET occupation information, and Mercor staff then reviewed each match. Candidates who passed this review completed an interest form reporting their occupation, years of experience, and location. We required at least two years of relevant experience for Personal Care Aides and Dishwashers, and at least four years for the other four occupations. Recruitment prioritized occupational fit and experience over representativeness. The sample is not stratified to match the U.S. workforce in the selected occupations (see Section C for sample characteristics). Workers were paid a minimum of $80 per hour, or at a higher market rate for their occupation. Participation on the platform was voluntary. This research was approved under IRB protocol 84069. Across six occupations, the TaskNet Interviewer conducted discovery interviews with 132 workers (Section 3.1) and collected task validations from 318 incumbents (Section 3.3), with modest demands on participants’ time. Discovery interviews lasted a median of 29 minutes (IQR: 19–46 minutes) 3 , with the shortest median durations among Dishwashers and Personal Care Aides (23 minutes) and the longest among Software Developers (43 minutes; Section C). Task validation took a comparable median of 28 minutes (IQR: 19–49 minutes), ranging from 16 minutes among Dishwashers to 40 minutes among Software Developers.

4.3 Task Overlap and Distinctiveness TaskNet overlaps substantially with O * NET tasks while also identifying tasks not already captured by the existing inventory (Figure 2). Of the 118 O * NET tasks, 88 ( 75% ) are covered by 123 tasks in TaskNet, as some existing tasks correspond to multiple tasks in TaskNet. The remaining 30 ( 25% ) are not covered, over a third of which are supplemental tasks. TaskNet not only covers existing tasks but also adds tasks absent from O * NET’s inventory. Of the 202 tasks in TaskNet, 79 ( 39% ) lack an identified O * NET counterpart (new). The share of new tasks varies across occupations, ranging from 15% for Dishwashers to 52% for Software Developers. Among the overlapping tasks, TaskNet often provides finer-grained descriptions of existing tasks (Figure 3). Of the 123 TaskNet tasks with an identified O * NET counterpart, 58 ( 47% ) refine existing task descriptions by capturing more specific activities (refined). The remaining 65 ( 53% ) overlap without providing additional granularity (related). We use an LLM judge to map these relationships (Section G.1). The first authors independently labeled 40 randomly sampled statements, agreeing on counterpart presence at 83% ( κ = 0.66 ) and the three-way relation at 70% ( κ = 0.53 ). Where the authors agreed, the judge matched their labels 85% and 71% of the time, respectively (Section G.2).

5 Task Inventory Validation Although task inventories underpin much of the research on the economic impact of AI, there has been no systematic way to assess them, since no definitive list establishes the scope of an occupation’s tasks or their appropriate granularity. We propose such a framework, evaluating any task inventory at two levels: the quality of individual statements and the representativeness of the inventory as a whole. At the statement level, expert review assesses task-writing quality and occupational fit (Section 5.1). At the inventory level, we compare TaskNet with O * NET version 31.0 on how well they represent work beyond the construction sample from six occupations. An internal evaluation tests coverage and cluster coherence on held-out worker reports collected through the same interview process (Section 5.2). An external evaluation tests coverage of employers’ descriptions of work in job postings (Section 5.2).
5.1 Task Statement Quality Every statement meets O * NET ’s standard for a task statement. Occupational analysts at the O * NET Centerreviewed 229 system-generated statements following Section 3.3 and judged every task statement to be a valid task. For comparison, 65.5% of initial write-in task suggestions provided by job incumbents and occupational experts were accepted as task statements in O * NET’s two most recent rounds of review (O * NET’s Analysis Cycles 26 and 27) (National Center for O*NET Development, 2026a). Although every statement was a valid task, analysts flagged some that departed from O * NET ’s writing guidelines or described work primarily performed by another occupation. Their feedback led us to rewrite 21% of statements (Section D). The first authors separately checked each statement against its underlying worker reports before review, revising 19% for fidelity. Alongside revisions to wording, O * NET analysts classified 11% of tasks as adjacent—valid tasks excluded from the 10
respective occupation’s task list due to occupational fit. The remaining 204 statements formed the primary list of occupational tasks. Workers recognize nearly every task as part of their work. Workers in each occupation rated the 204 occupational statements on O * NET’s dimensions of relevance, importance, and frequency. We retain statements that at least a quarter of workers rate as relevant to their occupation (Section 3.3), which removes two statements and leaves 202 . Of these statements, 180 ( 89% ) are core, against 82% of O * NET’s own tasks for these occupations (Table 1). The gap is largest for Software Developers (91% vs. 65%), Lawyers (88% vs. 68%), and Personal Care Aides (83% vs. 73%).
5.2 Inventory Representativeness To assess whether our inventories generalize beyond the interviews used to construct them, we compare TaskNet and the sampled occupations from O * NET 31.0 on two independent sources: internally, on tasks reported by workers held out from inventory construction, and externally, on tasks extracted from job postings. For internal evaluation, we interviewed 57 additional workers across the six occupations using the same recruitment and interview process. They reported 1184 tasks in total, none of which were used to build TaskNet. We assess both the breadth and organization of each inventory using coverage and silhouette score. Coverage is the share of held-out tasks an LLM judge finds described by at least one statement. Silhouette scores use task embeddings to assess whether tasks assigned to the same best-matching statement are more similar than those assigned elsewhere (Table 18). For external evaluation, we use 2026 U.S. job postings from Revelio Labs, drawing on a 1% random sample (Redivis, 2025) and supplementing it with 1000 randomly selected postings each for Personal Care Aides, Elementary School Teachers, and Emergency Medicine Physicians. We extract task sentences with the Job Ad Analysis Toolkit (JAAT) (Meisenbacher et al., 2025) and split them into single activities, yielding 12474 activities from 2186 postings. An LLM then judges whether each inventory contains a statement describing each activity. TaskNet covers more of the held-out tasks. Our inventories achieve higher coverage in five of the six occupations, averaging 89.3% compared with O * NET’s 78.6% (Table 2). These differences are significant in all sampled occupations except Dishwashers, where both inventories cover 85.7% of tasks. The gains are largest for Software Developers (17.0 points), Emergency Medicine Physicians ( 16.9 ), and Personal Care Aides ( 14.6 ), where O * NET leaves roughly a fifth to a third of the tasks workers report undescribed.

6 New, Refined, and Missing Tasks Task-based models describe technological change as the net effect of two forces: automation displaces labor from tasks it previously performed, while the creation of new tasks reinstates it (Acemoglu and Restrepo, 2019). The relation categories from Section 4.3 offer an initial view of both. New statements may signal emerging work, while missing tasks—O * NET tasks with no counterpart in TaskNet—may offer candidates for declining labor involvement or they may reflect methodological differences, such as sampling variation or O
*
NET’s use of multiple sources of task information. To characterize each category, the first authors read all of its statements and identified recurring themes. We defined each theme in a codebook with inclusion and exclusion rules and applied it by consensus (Section I). For comparison, we coded the 79 new statements together with the 65 related statements, and the 30 unconfirmed O * NET tasks together with the 88 covered ones, blind to category. Refined statements were coded against the O * NET task they refine. Because the themes were derived from the same statements they describe, the resulting comparisons show which features distinguish each category in our data rather than test hypotheses specified in advance. The themes are also not exhaustive, so some statements fall outside them, and others span several. New tasks surface invisible work. Every occupation includes work that keeps it running but seldom appears in formal descriptions of the job (Suchman, 1995). Star and Strauss (1999) describe such work as invisible: backgrounded activity that enables occupations to carry out their core function. Over half of new statements ( 53% ) fall into three themes that echo documented forms of invisible work, compared with about a third of related statements ( 34% ). The most distinctive is oversight and quality assurance ( 24% of new against 9% of related): tasks that maintain standards and establish accountability for the quality and safety of the work, such as Lawyers approving staff- drafted reports and filings or Physicians countersigning residents’ charts. The second is coordination ( 22% against 18% ), in which workers hand off tasks, information, and responsibility between people, across shifts, and from one stage to the next, such as Physicians receiving patient information at shift changes or Developers passing completed features to quality assurance teams. The third is teaching and professional development ( 11% against 8% ), tasks that sustain the expertise an occupation depends on, such as Physicians teaching residents or Personal Care Aides training staff in safe transfers.
13
Refined tasks clarify how work is structured and performed. Refined statements describe the core of each occupation (56 of 58 are core tasks). Refined statements add additional detail to their O * NET counterparts in two ways. 48% of our statements split an O * NET task into the steps or duties it bundles (e.g., Lawyers’ “represent clients in court or before government agencies” becomes drafting motions and briefs, preparing exhibits and witnesses, and presenting arguments). In 59% of the tasks, it specifies how a task is performed, through particular methods, tools, or standards (e.g., Personal Care Aides’ “Administer bedside or personal care, such as ambulation or personal hygiene assistance” becomes assisting clients with walking, transfers, and repositioning using mobility aids such as gait belts and ceiling lifts). The former reveals distinct duties within broad tasks, while the
latter clarifies the conditions and requirements of performing them. Missing tasks are O * NET’s least prevalent tasks. On O * NET’s own ratings, missing tasks are the ones its respondents report least often. 11 of the 30 missing tasks are supplemental, three times the share among covered tasks (37% against 11%). Our coding points the same way: 37% are specialized or dated, against 5% of covered tasks. Examples include Lawyers probating wills or serving as a trustee, guardian, or executor, and Dishwashers setting up banquet tables or packaging individual
place settings. O
*
NET may better capture such activities due to its sample. Technology creates new tasks and displaces old ones. 20% of new statements depend on a recent tool or practice, against 3% of shared ones. Technology enters the inventories in two ways. Sometimes it creates a task of its own, for example, Teachers reading and responding to email from colleagues or Developers building continuous integration and delivery pipelines. Technology also changes how existing tasks are done, for example, Teachers assigning computer-based activities to students. AI appears in the same two ways. For Software Developers, it creates new tasks such as designing prompts and evaluating model outputs. For Lawyers, it is a new object of existing review. Technology can also render older task descriptions obsolete. For instance, four of the 17 O * NET Software Developer tasks may predate current practice, such as “determine hardware configuration”, a decision that cloud platforms now largely abstract away.
4
7 Implications for AI Exposure Measurement Nearly every AI exposure estimate relies on task inventories, making the choice of inventory consequential for measuring AI’s potential labor market impacts. Conceptually, AI exposure measures the degree to which AI capabilities overlap with the activities involved in a task (Felten et al., 2021, Webb, 2020). Exposure estimates therefore depend on how tasks are defined and represented in an inventory. TaskNet matches O * NET’s standards while covering more work in finer detail, making it a natural basis for revisiting exposure estimates. We use two established measures of AI exposure that rate each task based on its written description and average across tasks within each occupation. Eloundou- β (Eloundou et al., 2024) captures whether access to a large language model would cut the time needed to complete a task by at least half, counting tasks that also require additional software at half weight (0–1 scale). RL feasibility (Tomei and Teeselink, 2026) uses a rubric to assess how feasible it is to train language models on a task through reinforcement learning (0–100 scale), based on dimensions including machine access, environment simulability, output gradeability, feedback frequency, and sequential decision

8 Discussion Understanding how AI changes work requires an up-to-date account of what people do in their jobs. This paper makes five contributions toward such an account. First, we introduce the TaskNet Interviewer, a system that elicits tasks from incumbents through AI-conducted interviews with adaptive task probing and verifies them through worker review (Section 3.1). Second, we present an aggregation framework that makes explicit two choices that most inventories make implicitly— whether different reports describe the same task and how finely tasks should be defined (Section 3.2). It defines task identity through hierarchical task analysis and task granularity through functional job analysis (Fine and Cronshaw, 1999, Stanton, 2006), and applies these definitions in an iterative procedure that resolves overlaps and preserves coverage of the reported work. Third, since task lists have no ground truth, we propose an evaluation framework that triangulates across O * NET Center Analysts, incumbents, worker ratings, and job postings (Section 5). Fourth, we release validated inventories for six occupations: O * NET Center Analysts judged all statements to be valid task statements, and incumbents endorsed all but two of the 204 as relevant. Finally, we show that AI exposure estimates differ between TaskNet and O * NET, with higher estimates under TaskNet for Lawyers and Software Developers and lower estimates for Personal Care Aides (Section 7).
8.1 Explaining Differences in AI Exposure Estimates Substituting TaskNet for O * NET changes exposure estimates, with new tasks accounting for much of the difference (Section 7). Three channels may explain this difference: task discovery methods, data collection periods, and worker samples. Our design cannot isolate each channel’s respective contribution, so we discuss the evidence supporting each and its limitations. Task Discovery Methods. O * NET’s surveys ask incumbents to rate statements that already exist, and new tasks enter only through write-ins and Analyst review (Dierdorff and Norton, 2011, Klein et al., 2025). In contrast, TaskNet uses open-ended interviews that allow workers to describe their activities in their own words, with follow-ups to surface additional tasks (Section 3.1). Under this explanation, “new” tasks are not necessarily newly emerging or increasingly performed tasks, but existing tasks that are newly documented. Over half of the new statements concern such invisible tasks, which contribute to the difference in exposure scores. These are activities that keep an occupation running but seldom appear in formal descriptions of a job (Star and Strauss, 1999). TaskNet therefore captures AI-exposed work that existing inventories miss. The high exposure of invisible tasks is notable because they typically draw on tacit knowledge and are difficult to fully automate. Work that is difficult to observe or articulate may still be exposed to AI, even if human judgment, accountability, and relationships may remain essential and prevent full automation. Hence, the extent to which AI replaces rather than supports human work depends not only on technical feasibility but also on how organizations choose to deploy it. Task Collection Periods. While we selected occupations whose O * NET task information was updated recently (between 2023 and 2025), work may have evolved since, and O * NET’s discovery process adds new tasks only in later survey cycles (Section 1). Some new statements do reflect genuinely recent work: 20% depend on a recent tool or practice, against 3% of related statements, and new technology is one theme behind the exposure difference. For these statements, “new” does mean newly performed. The high exposure of these tasks may partly reflect priorities of model 16
developers. AI and related digital tools create new activities, such as prompt design and model evaluation, that align closely with the capabilities and environments developers are optimizing for. Worker Sampling. Finally, the inventories may differ because they draw on different worker samples. TaskNet recruits workers through an AI data platform based on occupational fit and experience (Section 4.1), whereas O * NET draws on multiple sampling frames, including business establishments, professional associations, and specialized occupational listings. These approaches may reach workers with different roles and experiences, potentially affecting which tasks are reported. Notably, O * NET tasks missing from TaskNet are more often specialized or dated than covered tasks ( 37% versus 5% ). The omission of these tasks contributes to differences in AI exposure estimates.
8.2 Limitations and Future Work
Our approach has several limitations. First, constructing task inventories requires judgments about task specificity and occupational fit. Although our task definition draws on existing theory (Fine and Cronshaw, 1999, Stanton, 2006), it cannot eliminate subjectivity in determining task boundaries. Similarly, judgments about occupational fit may exclude relevant tasks: 81% of the statements analysts judged adjacent still met our task criterion, and more than half were core (Section D.1). Such tasks may fall outside prevailing occupational definitions even as they become more important in practice. These choices affect downstream measures, as specificity determines how work is represented in task averages, while occupational fit determines which activities are counted. Second, although our inventories represent our sample well, roughly twenty workers per occupation recruited through a single platform may not capture the full range of occupational tasks. Expanding beyond six occupations would enable broader validation and help establish whether task-based exposure predicts short-term labor market outcomes (Brynjolfsson et al., 2025a, Lichtinger and Hosseini Maasoum, 2025) or long-term employment projections (Massenkoff and McCrory, 2026). Third, our task inventories capture individual activities but omit workers’ preferences and broader attributes, including knowledge, skills, and abilities. By representing tasks as unordered lists, they also overlook how activities interact within workflows, even though these relationships shape how automation affects production (Demirer et al., 2026, Gilbreth and Gilbreth, 1921, Hammer, 1990, Malone and Crowston, 1994). Future work could use AI-guided interviews to capture both the human and organizational context surrounding tasks. Despite these limitations, our study offers a proof of concept for using worker interviews to doc- ument tasks at scale and modest expense. Scaling our method across occupations could support more current and detailed representations of work, as a stronger empirical foundation for anticipat- ing changes in skill demand and guiding economic policy. AI may be driving an unprecedented transformation of work. Our information infrastructure for understanding this transformation must advance alongside it.
